title: A second collapsed lung in a young non-smoker
chief_complaint: Sudden left-sided chest pain and breathlessness
vignette: A 32-year-old woman who has never smoked comes to the emergency department with sudden, sharp left-sided chest pain and breathlessness that began while she was carrying shopping upstairs. Eighteen months ago she had a right-sided spontaneous pneumothorax treated with a chest drain. Since then she has noticed that she gets breathless on hills sooner than her friends.

decisions.prompt: What else do you ask her?
decisions.explanation: A second pneumothorax with slowly progressive breathlessness in a young woman calls for a cystic lung disease history: smoking, hormones, kidney lesions and features of tuberous sclerosis.

options.text: Does she take any hormonal medication?
options.reveal: A combined oestrogen-progestogen pill for six years.

options.text: Has she ever had kidney problems or flank pain?
options.reveal: Two years ago an ultrasound found a fatty lump in her left kidney; nobody followed it up.

options.text: Has she or anyone in her family had seizures or unusual skin lesions?

options.feedback: Travel does not explain a recurrent pneumothorax with progressive breathlessness.
options.reveal: A beach holiday in Spain last summer.

options.text: Did she have eczema as a child?
options.reveal: Mild eczema that cleared by age ten.

decisions.prompt: Which diagnoses do you keep open?
decisions.explanation: Recurrent pneumothorax in a young never-smoker points to a diffuse cystic lung disease. Lymphangioleiomyomatosis and Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome lead; Langerhans cell histiocytosis is almost confined to smokers.

options.feedback: Almost exclusively seen in smokers; she has never smoked.

options.text: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax with otherwise normal lungs
options.feedback: A second episode plus progressive breathlessness makes an underlying lung disease likely.
Does not explain a recurrent pneumothorax.

decisions.explanation: High-resolution CT shows the cysts; a serum VEGF-D above 800 pg/mL with typical cysts is diagnostic, so a biopsy can be avoided. Abdominal imaging looks for angiomyolipoma; lung function sets the baseline for treatment decisions.

options.feedback: Points towards sarcoidosis, which does not cause thin-walled cysts and recurrent pneumothorax.

options.text: Surgical lung biopsy as the first test
options.feedback: Typical CT cysts with a raised VEGF-D are diagnostic; surgical biopsy adds risk without benefit.

decisions.explanation: Recurrent pneumothorax, diffuse thin-walled cysts, a renal angiomyolipoma and a VEGF-D above 800 pg/mL in a young woman establish lymphangioleiomyomatosis without a biopsy. Oestrogen exposure can accelerate it.

decisions.prompt: What is your plan for her?
decisions.explanation: Treat the pneumothorax and offer pleurodesis after a second episode, start sirolimus because lung function is declining, remove exogenous oestrogen and vaccinate. Corticosteroids do not help, and more oestrogen may speed progression.
